item.text: {"piece_id":"01","title":"CAD AI Moves Into the Workflow, but the Checks Still Lag","question":"What changed, and which developments matter most to this audience?","argument":"The meaningful shift is from AI demonstrations toward CAD-adjacent workflow tools: text-generated custom features, visual retrieval of existing models, simulation setup from CAD, and tested drawing-to-CAD conversion. These developments can reduce modeling and handoff work, but they do not yet make generated geometry production-ready by default. The strongest near-term opportunity is supervised first-draft and retrieval work inside native engineering systems, with explicit geometry, tolerance, simulation-input, and manufacturing checks retained.","synthesis":"Commercial CAD vendors are productizing AI at the interfaces around geometry—search, reusable FeatureScript tools, and simulation setup—while Engineering.com’s Backflip test supplies a narrower independent check on one geometry-generation workflow. Taken together, the evidence suggests that the practical change is not autonomous engineering: it is a growing set of assisted entry points into existing CAD and simulation environments. The parallel robotics evidence reinforces the same distinction: NVIDIA’s CAD-to-simulation workflow checks asset scale, joints, collision geometry, and grasp behavior in simulation, which is more concrete than visual plausibility but still does not establish physical transfer or manufacturing fitness.","limitations":"The most direct independent CAD test covers only two successful, relatively simple speed-modeling drawings and one failed multibody drawing; it cannot establish performance on shop drawings, tolerance-critical parts, or real production workflows. Most other evidence is vendor reporting about released or planned capabilities, so teams need their own representative test sets and release
